title: A glossary term's own fields — software-analysis capability
description: One entry of the glossary, `glossary.md` under the analysis location (software-analysis DEC-001 points 1 to 3): a domain word and what it means. The entry is keyed by the term's id (`analysis.schema.json#/$defs/term-id`), which sits outside this object and is separate from the display name, so renaming a term breaks nothing that cites it: the new name goes in `name` and the old one into `replaces`. Its body section is the one headed by the id. These are the entry's own fields: its friction block sits in the methodology's container beside them and is the core's (COR-050, COR-053 point 10). A term anchors to where the software or a decision embodies it (DEC-001 point 4); one nothing embodies carries the reason it has none as `unanchored-because` in its friction block, the core's key, never among these fields (DEC-001 point 9; COR-050 point 1). Applied by the capability's check, `pkit software-analysis validate`; unknown fields are refused.

name.description: The term as it is written today.

definition.description: What the term means: a phrase that could stand in for the term, its broader kind and then what sets it apart (DEC-001 point 1). The kind's declared structure gives it the form `definition` (`artefact-kinds.yaml`).

replaces.description: The names the term was written as before, newest first — the record of renames (DEC-001 point 1). Only names it carried in the analysis or in an accepted record. A working name that now means something else is one of the words the term could be confused with.

noun-forms.description: Other forms of the term's name as a noun, such as its plural, each one that cannot read as a verb, such as `payments` and never `orders` (DEC-001 point 1). A language that inflects its nouns lists more, such as their cases. Each is one of the term's names, so no other term takes it, and the links between terms take it as a mention of the term (software-analysis DEC-004 point 7).

other-senses.description: Each phrase in which the term's name has another sense, one its distinctions tell apart, such as `in order to` beside the `order` a customer places (DEC-001 point 1). No link names the term inside such a phrase (software-analysis DEC-004 point 7). Each holds one of the term's names, and more.
